Strategic Framework

The Invisible Funnel

Buyers now discover, evaluate, and decide before we ever see them. Here's what that means for PMM.

By the time most buyers reach SAP directly, an AI system has likely already framed their problem, shortlisted the players, and formed a preference—all long before a lead, a form fill, or a sales conversation gives us any visibility into that decision.

This isn't a forecast about some future disruption. The evidence shows it's already underway, and it's an industry-wide shift. Organic search traffic to SAP.com is down 15.8% year over year. Sales-relevant hand-raiser actions are down 13.8%. Organic's share of inbound traffic has fallen from 34% to 27%.

The funnel we've always used to map the buyer journey makes it look linear and connected. But the buyer's journey is rarely either. It doesn't move in sequence—stages overlap, circle back, and happen concurrently. And increasingly, they happen before we can see them.

68%
of buyers already have a front-runner in mind before a vendor even knows a deal exists—and that front-runner wins 80% of the time.

This is a buyer-behavior story, not just an AI story

It would be easy to read this as an argument about AI. But that would miss the point.

Buyers have long self-directed their research, consulted third parties before vendors, and arrived at preferences before any visible engagement. These behaviors were documented years before generative AI entered the mainstream. Forrester frames the whole modern buying journey as "a process of confirmation, not selection"—a description of how people decide, not of any technology.

AI is the accelerant, not the fire. What was already happening—self-directed buyer research, early preference formation, third-party validation—has been made faster, more comprehensive, and harder to observe.

Nine in ten business buyers now use generative AI or conversational search somewhere in their process, hiding signals that used to be visible to us. Among buyers of purchases of $1 million or more, GenAI usage reaches 97%—which is directly relevant to both our Enterprise and Corporate segments.

"AI answer engines function less like a search engine and more like upper-funnel media—closer to a billboard—generating brand-halo effects outside any property a brand owns."
— Forrester Research

Where discovery now begins

For most of the last two decades, SAP's digital business ran on a simple assumption: buyers search, click, and land somewhere we can measure. That assumption is broken.

Forrester forecasts B2B organic traffic declining 50% to 75% over the next 18 months. Click-through engagement on links in AI answer engines is only hitting 2% to 4%, against a historical keyword-search average of nearly 40%. As of early 2026, 68% of US Google searches ended without a click—the fastest two-year acceleration SparkToro has recorded.

What replaces the vanishing clicks isn't silence; it's influence moving elsewhere. Discovery increasingly happens inside AI systems that draw on owned platforms, customer advocacy content, and third-party ecosystems like LinkedIn, Reddit, and YouTube.

The compounding effect

Once a competitor becomes the repeated reference point for a concept, their authority compounds and displacing them gets harder. This is exactly why PMMs need to understand and act on this shift now—before these patterns harden.

Preference forms before the funnel can see it

If discovery has moved upstream, so has the decision itself.

Forrester's research is blunt: most B2B buying is "a process of confirmation, not selection." The deals our funnel shows us were, more often than not, substantially decided before they entered our field of view.

But early preference isn't fixed, and AI is what unsettles it. Among buyers with a single preferred vendor, 21% who used GenAI tools ultimately switched—more than double the 8% switch rate among those who didn't. Being the incumbent front-runner is a real advantage, but GenAI makes it meaningfully more contestable.

That cuts both ways. SAP has put real effort into correcting a reputation earned over years. AI-mediated discovery rewards current proof over incumbency bias more than traditional search ever did. If our proof is strong and consistently represented, that dynamic gives SAP a faster, more credible path to reset outdated perceptions.

What this means for PMM

Marketing's job is no longer just to capture and convert a visible lead. It's to make sure SAP is accurately understood, credibly evidenced, and consistently considered before that observable buying process ever begins.

This reframing carries direct implications for how we work:

  • Content becomes infrastructure, not just assets. The answer isn't more content—it's a coherent system of approved messaging and proof that AI systems can reliably retrieve and represent.
  • Third-party presence matters more than ever. Buyers trust industry peers (72%) and analysts (68%) more than a provider's own executives (66%). Partner-facing enablement now doubles as buyer-facing influence.
  • Measurement must expand beyond the funnel. We need visibility into preference formation before a lead exists, not just lead capture.
  • Speed becomes critical. Forrester documented model behavior and citation patterns shifting weekly—faster than quarterly planning can track. Annual planning and quarterly reporting were built for a world that changed slowly enough for those cadences to keep up. It no longer does.

The connected marketing system

The strategic response isn't a new platform or a new team. It's a connected marketing system—the governed messaging, research, proof points, and content that shape how buyers discover and evaluate SAP.

In practice, this means:

  • Approved messaging and proof: One current, approved, searchable source for product language, claims, terminology, and customer proof.
  • Retrievability: Structuring that material so people and AI systems can find it wherever they look—on our properties, in third-party ecosystems, and inside AI answer engines.
  • Governance: Tiered messaging governance that distinguishes fundamental narrative changes from product-level updates or editorial improvements.
  • Connected signals: Joining first-party funnel data with upstream evidence from AI visibility, brand perception, and third-party presence.

This is not a move away from campaigns or from marketers. It's a move toward a foundation that makes campaigns more effective and gives marketers the infrastructure they need to compete in an environment where influence forms before the funnel can see it.

The opportunity

Our SEO, Content Hub, and web investments already have SAP's declines running favorably against the industry benchmark. We're better positioned than most competitors to close the distance—and, in some cases, to jump to the front of the pack. The question is whether we act on that position.

Why this matters for your work

Every capability in the Book of Work connects to this shift. Whether you're building competitive intelligence, crafting messaging frameworks, or enabling sales—the work increasingly determines whether SAP shows up in buyer discovery, not just whether we convert leads that arrive.

The AI tools and skills we're building through NextGen PMM aren't just about efficiency. They're about operating at the speed this new environment demands—and ensuring our messaging and proof is consistently represented wherever buyers and AI systems look.

The invisible funnel isn't something we can unravel or reclaim. The more useful response isn't to fight the shift, but to find the opportunity inside it.
